title: random consumer api
body:
`TCache` `RandomConsumer` api was not good previously: 
- consumer could read from arbitrary offsets in `TCache` by calling `read_at(seq)`
- consumer had to track minimum seq in use and call consumer `set_tail` to free cache entries

Now: 
- consumer 'acquires' a `TCacheRead`
- acquired read gives access to the underlying buffer
- tail is updated automatically when the acquired read is dropped

```
let acquired: TRead = ra_consumer.acquire(t_cache_read);
let data = acquired.buffer()?;
...
```

1. 
```
thread '<unnamed>' (72057) panicked at crates/common/src/spine/stream_id.rs:86:18:
misaligned pointer dereference: address must be a multiple of 0x8 but is 0x1
```
when a slot was skipped the `TCache` `Consumer` would return an empty buffer - in the gossip tile we try to dereference the buffer as a `P2pStreadId` without checking the length. 

Fix: skip the skipped slots in the consumer - never return an empty buffer. 

2.

thread '<unnamed>' (84446) panicked at crates/common/src/spine/tcache.rs:143:9:
100432192 - 60653568 > 33554432

The cache consumer had run more than buffer length bytes ahead of a consumer. The issue here is that the the consumer had never published its tail sequence b/c it was stuck in a consume loop reading a large set of synced blocks and `free()` (which publishes the tail seq) was only being called once consuming has finished.

Fix: add `auto_free` option on the `RandomAccessConsumer` so that the tail is published every time an `AcquiredRead` is dropped.

this change adds a window over which messages may be out of order.

title: [CL-111] Attestation aggregation: in-tile pool, admission gaps, and aggregate-topic verification shedding
body:
Two halves:

* Network-level aggregation: gossip-verified `SingleAttestation`s incrementally BLS-aggregate per (slot, committee, data root) into one-committee `Attestation`s, serialized in the future `GET aggregate_attestation` shape; verification returns its artifacts so aggregation adds zero re-hashing/re-parsing; subnet-consistency REJECT and per-(attester, epoch) first-seen IGNORE close the singles-topic admission gaps.
* Aggregate-topic performance (CL-111): per-(aggregator, epoch) first-seen and spec superset-coverage IGNOREs now shed redundant aggregates on bitset/byte compares before the ~1 ms three-signature batch verify — the common case at 16 aggregators/committee — while union-covered messages still verify and relay, skipping only the redundant local vote fold.

All admission structures are bounded, slot-pruned, `#[timed]` where the repo's granularity rule says, and covered by direct lifecycle tests plus handler-level tests including structural proofs (corrupted-signature-subset → Ignore) and an e2e oracle through `handle_aggregate_and_proof`

Also defined `BeaconStateCounters`, currently used for `SeenAggregatesFull` and `AttestationPoolFull`; may want to define more in the future.

title: Precompute fork-data roots for BLS domain derivation
body:
`bls::compute_domain` recomputed `hash_tree_root_fork_data` — a hash of two values that never change after boot — on every gossip message and per item inside several block-body loops (~1,900 instructions / a few hundred ns per call). Both inputs are boot-knowable: `genesis_validators_root` is process- constant, and the complete set of fork versions a process can ever see is the loaded state's `Fork` pair plus the pinned genesis/capella/gloas versions (`fork_version_at` only selects within the Fork pair, and `upgrade_to_gloas` only rotates current→previous and installs the boot-known gloas version).

So these are derived constants. `Immutable` now computes the five fork-data roots (3 hardcoded + previous + current) once at construction, and `fork_data_root(version)` is a total lookup — a five-entry compare with a compute-on-miss fallback plus debug log, so an unexpected version can only cost the old latency, never correctness. No invalidation exists anywhere; `upgrade_to_gloas` needs zero awareness. Because the roots travel inside `Immutable`, every cross-tile state view gets them for free.

All 15 production `compute_domain` sites become a `domain_from_fork_data` splice over the lookup, and the aggregate path's per-message fork-data hash becomes the same lookup. `verify_single_attestation`, `verify_block_signature` and `signing_root_for_block_header` take the domain directly instead of `(fork_version, genesis_validators_root)`; loop-invariant domains hoist out of the exit, BLS-change and proposer-slashing per-item loops. Net -21 lines of production code; the change introduces zero comments.

Measured (perf-local A/B on the committed 128-block fixtures, hardware instruction counters — wall-clock deltas at this scale are noise):

| | baseline | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `compute_domain` | 1,041 calls, 1.98M instr | 0 calls |
| `hash_tree_root_fork_data` | 1,044 calls, 711k instr | 13 calls (boot refreshes), 13.5k instr |
| `collect_sigs_block_body` | 1,095.7M instr | −16.7k instr/block (−0.195%) |
| whole block pipeline | ~368M instr/block | ≈ −0.004% |

This not really a performance improvement change - even though the win is real and measurable, it is too small to have an impact. This is primarily a simplification/refactoring PR.

The `#[timed]` instrumentation commit that enabled the measurement is kept: the `collect_sigs_*` frames are durable per the repo's timing conventions, and `compute_domain`'s own frame now proves its absence from hot paths.

Testing: new data-crate tests assert the roots are precomputed (via the private field, so the total accessor can't mask a broken refresh), the fallback path, and a decompose round-trip with a distinct gvr + Fork pair. All pre-existing tests pass unmodified — signing is byte-identical by construction.

title: Add CONTEXT.md, the project glossary for humans and coding agents
body:
The file follows the domain-modeling convention from Matt Pocock's skills collection for AI coding agents (github.com/mattpocock/skills). Its principles, briefly:

- One canonical term per concept, chosen deliberately; the synonyms a reader might reach for are listed under "Avoid". Vocabulary drift -- "service" here, "worker" there, for the same thing -- is how naming fragments over time, and coding agents drift faster than humans do.
- A definition says what a thing IS, in one or two sentences. The file is a glossary only: no implementation details, no spec, no scratch pad. Those live in docs/ and in the code.
- It grows lazily. A term is added when it crystallises in design or review, never speculatively; an entry that has to be argued about is an entry that was added too early.
- It serves agents as much as people: agent tooling built on these skills reads the glossary before exploring the codebase and sticks to its vocabulary in everything it produces -- code, issue text, review comments -- so generated output speaks the project's language instead of inventing its own.

Silver benefits more than most: tile, spine, and TCache read as generic English but name precise architectural commitments here, and the glossary is where that precision is pinned.

The sibling convention, decision records under docs/adr/, records choices that are hard to reverse, surprising without context, and the result of a real trade-off. The first ADRs arrive with the Beacon API work (#81), where both conventions are already in day-to-day use.

title: Document the decoupling and cohesion rules
body:
The tile boundaries, the crate tiers, and the spine's producer/consumer contract are enforced by review alone. An upward edge inside the tier DAG compiles. Every tile holds a producer for every queue, so producing a message another tile owns runs. The shared state reader is handed out at construction with nothing marking which values may ride it. None of that is visible from the code that depends on it.

docs/decoupling-rules.md states what may cross a boundary: fourteen rules, each naming what enforces it — the compiler for three, Cargo for one, review for one, nothing at all for seven. That column is the point. A reviewer needs to know where the compiler helps and where attention is the only mechanism.

docs/cohesion-rules.md covers the scales above CLAUDE.md's encapsulation section: what earns a tile, a crate, a file, a type.

Both close with a table of the places the codebase departs from its own rules — the tier edge that exists for one constant, the hosted crate that touches the spine, the counter namespace filed under another crate's. The documents are meant to be falsifiable, not aspirational.

docs/spine-message-flow.md gains the sentence that makes its queue table's standing explicit: those columns are the only statement of who may produce what, so a topology change updates them.

CLAUDE.md points at both from the project-shape list.

QUIC stack copies all outbound data into ack buffers in case it needs to resend. This change removes those allocations for outbound gossip - instead we pass in tcache references. 

This requires that the tcache data lives until the sent data is acked and must not be released. The default `RandomAccessConsumer` is not strict in this regard and can release acquired data if it falls behind; so this PR adds a 'strict' mode where this behaviour is not allowed. Only used currently on the outbound gossip consumer.

title: Add bounded chunked responses to httpcore
body:
`ServerConnection` frames response bodies with `Content-Length`. Server-sent events need a response that stays open as more data arrives. This PR adds `ChunkedResponse` to support that lifetime, with HTTP chunked framing and bounded buffers.

`ServerConnection::into_stream` transfers the queued response head and buffers into `ChunkedResponse`. The head is sent before any appended chunks. Buffered pipelined requests are abandoned, and subsequent input is discarded. The connection cannot be reused, and closes without a terminal chunk.

The transition reserves a 64 KiB send buffer and trims the inherited read buffer to 4 KiB of discard scratch. Accepted pushes do not reallocate. The unsent-byte limit includes the response head and chunk framing; a push exceeding it is refused, requiring the caller to close the connection.

The machine also tracks time without write progress while output is pending. The caller supplies both the clock and deadline, and decides when to close a stalled connection. This measures writes accepted by the socket, not reads by the peer.

Direct machine tests cover framing, partial writes, buffer limits and allocation stability, stall timing, and the transition from request parsing to discarding input.

The stacked PR adds the first consumer: block subscriptions at `/eth/v1/events`. Topic selection, event publication, and connection expiry policy belong there.

title: Serve block events over SSE at /eth/v1/events
body:
`/eth/v1/events` previously returned 404. This PR lets clients subscribe to the `block` topic and receive newly imported blocks over SSE. It builds on the chunked response machine from #220.

A successful subscription keeps the existing socket and transitions the connection from request handling to a subscription backed by `ChunkedResponse`. Each block event is rendered once and queued for subscribers. Quiet subscriptions survive the ordinary HTTP idle timeout. A shared timer queues keep-alive comments every 15 seconds.

A subscriber is closed if a frame would exceed the 64 KiB unsent-byte limit. The expiry sweep also closes connections with pending output after more than 12 seconds without socket write progress. This deadline is separate from request idle and linger timeouts.

The application-boundary tile publishes blocks from `BlockReceived { stage: Applied }` notifications. Events carry `execution_optimistic: true` because publication precedes the execution payload verdict.

Repeated receipts now produce `BlockStage::AlreadyKnown` when the root is already in fork choice. This prevents those receipts from publishing another block event, without a downstream deduplication cache. The sync engine treats them as applied coverage, while the stages reader ignores them. Storage continues to receive the separate `PersistBlock` notification.

Topic parameters may be comma-separated or repeated. Unsupported topics, including empty entries, reject the whole subscription with HTTP 400 and an error naming the topic. Missing `topics` also returns 400. Error messages use JSON string escaping to preserve client-supplied names safely.

Only `block` is supported. Clients requesting `head` or other topics receive 400; this PR does not provide all events needed by validator clients.

ADR-0004 records the separation between request handling and streaming. Tests cover:

- Topic parsing, subscription responses, and JSON-escaped errors through the router.
- Delivery over TCP and Unix sockets, keep-alives, output limits, stall expiry, disconnects, and discarded pipelined requests.
- Delivery through the tile’s spine consumer, with publication restricted to `Applied`.
- Producer and consumer handling of `AlreadyKnown`, including importing an EF fixture block and receiving it again.

The fixture test requires `ef_tests` and readable fixtures. Its initial import bypasses proposer-signature verification because the checkpoint lacks decompressed public keys.

title: Serve `head` and `head_v2` events over SSE
body:
Adds `head` and `head_v2` to `/eth/v1/events`, alongside `block`. Both topics report changes to the selected head or its execution optimism. Validating an optimistic head, for example, produces another event for the same block with `execution_optimistic: false`.

`head_v2` also reports changes in fork choice's empty/full payload selection, including both transition directions. These can occur without changing the head block or its optimism. Its versioned response identifies the configured fork at the head block's slot; selected pre-Gloas blocks report `full`.

The existing `BeaconStateEvent::Status` carries the head's state root, both dependent roots and payload resolution as one coherent observation. Additional publications cover head changes outside block import, including execution verdicts. Consumers decide which observations require action; `/eth/v1/node/syncing` also receives prompt optimism updates.

The application boundary suppresses repeated observations. The first complete observation establishes a baseline, and subscribers receive future changes without an initial snapshot. `epoch_transition` is true only when the observed head epoch advances. If checkpoint history has overwritten a required dependent root, publication waits for a complete observation and retains the previous baseline.

The checkpoint anchor now advertises its block header's slot. Previously, a checkpoint state advanced through empty slots could advertise the later state slot instead.

Memory cost: the beacon-events ring grows from 3 MiB to 5 MiB, with event size increasing from 144 to 240 bytes and queue slots from 192 to 320 bytes. Retaining the state root adds 32 bytes per fork-choice node. Payload resolution fits the event's padding and adds no further ring growth.

Tests cover head and payload transitions, dependent-root history and checkpoint boundaries, repeated Status consumers, replay gating, fork-version selection, and delivery to individual and mixed-topic subscribers. Slot and PTC tests exercise publication from controlled fork-choice inputs; signed envelope and PTC gossip validation are outside those tests.

Validation: formatting, clippy and diff checks passed; `just nextest` passed 1,382 tests with five skipped. Subsequent prose edits passed formatting and diff checks.

title: Serve `block_gossip` events for gossip publication requests
body:
Add `block_gossip` to `/eth/v1/events`. The promise is: **these events correspond to what we publish on gossip**. An event reports silver's publication request, not successful delivery to a peer.

This deliberately narrows the [Beacon API's validation event](https://github.com/ethereum/beacon-APIs/blob/ef98d512c03c8ca6b9d7cbdc45b9293ec2b24722/apis/eventstream/index.yaml#L73-L77). Upstream covers blocks received through P2P or API after gossip validation, without requiring publication. Silver additionally requires a relay request, so validated RPC imports and disk replay produce no `block_gossip` event.

A request precedes payload notification, state transition, and import; a later import failure does not retract it. The existing `block` topic remains tied to `Applied` receipts. Repeated requests are not deduplicated, and late subscribers receive no replay. The two queues establish no shared ordering; subscribing to both topics can reach the existing send cap sooner.

```text
event: block_gossip
data: {"slot":"<decimal>","block":"0x<64 lowercase hex>"}
```

This PR targets `main`; `bronek/sse_data_column_sidecar_v2` follows. Neither PR depends on PR #231 or its head topics.

- **Carry block metadata on gossip relay requests:** attach slot and root at both existing relay sites. Producer and Controller tests cover selection, import receipts, routing, and IWANT service.
- **Serve block_gossip events over SSE:** add the topic, renderer, and boundary consumer outside the engine capacity gate. Socket tests cover isolation, repeats, late subscribers, and engine saturation.

The [ADR-0004 amendment](docs/adr/0004-sync-materialized-api.md) records the publication contract and deliberate divergence. P2P conformance gaps remain tracked separately.

Message sizes and ring capacities are unchanged.

Coverage limits: no Gloas fixture exercises the full `AwaitParentPayload` retry with its envelope. The proposer-lookahead test bypasses signatures. Relay tests require `ef_tests`, enabled by `just nextest`.

title: Serve `data_column_sidecar` events for gossip publication requests
body:
Add `data_column_sidecar` to `/eth/v1/events`. The promise is: **these events correspond to what we publish on gossip**. An event reports silver's publication request, not successful delivery to a peer.

This PR uses [Beacon API v5.0.0-alpha.2](https://github.com/ethereum/beacon-APIs/releases/tag/v5.0.0-alpha.2) as its specification baseline, rather than released v4.0.0.

This deliberately narrows [the alpha's validation event](https://github.com/ethereum/beacon-APIs/blob/v5.0.0-alpha.2/apis/eventstream/index.yaml#L162-L166). Upstream covers sidecars received through P2P or API after subnet gossip validation. Silver additionally requires publication, intentionally coupling these notifications to relay policy.

Both publication paths follow silver's gossip checks, including KZG. Gossip columns request `SendGossip`; RPC columns request `PublishDataColumn` while synced, regardless of custody. Buffered copies remain silent after their missing block or parent arrives. Syncing RPC, held copies, and EL reconstruction also remain silent. A later acquisition or encoding failure does not retract the original request.

```text
event: data_column_sidecar
data: {"block_root":"0x<64 lowercase hex>","index":"<decimal>","slot":"<decimal>"}
```

**Compatibility:** clients requiring v4's `kzg_commitments` field cannot decode this event. Silver follows the alpha's three-field payload, introduced in [`v5.0.0-alpha.1`](https://github.com/ethereum/beacon-APIs/blob/v5.0.0-alpha.1/apis/eventstream/index.yaml). [#583](https://github.com/ethereum/beacon-APIs/pull/583) removed `kzg_commitments` on 2026-03-09 after Gloas removed commitments from sidecars; Fulu sidecars still carry them. Released `v4.0.0` retains the field. The [inspected go-eth2-client checkout](https://github.com/attestantio/go-eth2-client/blob/85ac0f6e00e8230c030d9756350ea5e4acd52d2c/api/v1/datacolumnsidecarevent.go) (2026-07-16) and Lighthouse v8.2.2 use the v4 event shape. go-eth2-client rejects an empty commitments array; Lighthouse requires both `kzg_commitments` and `versioned_hashes`. Consumers using these decoders, including Xatu and ethereum-metrics-exporter, need v5 support to decode this event.

 This PR stacks on `bronek/sse_block_gossip_v2`, as the second PR above `main`. It has no prerequisite on PR #231.

- **Carry column metadata on publication requests:** introduce the metadata enum and enrich both existing requests. Producer tests cover selection, metadata, persistence, and completion; Controller tests verify routing and that conversion adds no second spine publication.
- **Serve data_column_sidecar events over SSE:** add the topic, renderer, and boundary handling for both request variants. Socket tests cover all three topics, repeats, late subscribers, and engine saturation.
- **Clean up temporary test directories and shared memory:** give fixtures cleanup owners and unlink Flux objects before removing their link files. This includes pre-existing test leaks found while reviewing the stack.
- **Let rust-analyzer see every feature:** a root `rust-analyzer.toml` mirroring `just clippy`'s `--all-features`, so feature-gated test support stops showing as unresolved imports in editors.
 
The cleanup commit covers normal teardown and unwinding. Process-global timer objects and cleanup after aborts remain separate work.

`Persist`, `Available`, and their consumers remain unchanged. Repeated requests are not deduplicated; late subscribers receive no replay. Additional subscriptions can reach the existing send cap sooner.

The [ADR-0004 amendment](docs/adr/0004-sync-materialized-api.md) records the publication contract and deliberate divergence. P2P conformance gaps remain tracked separately.
Message sizes and ring capacities are unchanged.

Coverage limits:

- Synthetic Fulu fixtures pre-seed the signature cache because their validator registry is empty; parent, proposer, inclusion, and KZG checks still run.
- Staged-parent assertions require installed EF fixtures; the test returns early when they are absent.

title: Write SSE frames eagerly and raise the send cap to 512 KiB
body:
`/eth/v1/events` subscriptions queued frames until `handle_event`. A publication burst could exceed the 64 KiB send cap in `fan_out` and disconnect subscribers **while their sockets still had room**.

This PR attempts socket writes as frames are published inside `fan_out` and raises the cap to 512 KiB. With no earlier event backlog, that accommodates one block’s 128 column events carrying 21 Fulu `kzg_commitments` each (about 290 KiB) even when the socket accepts no bytes. It prepares the transport for the follow-up PR adding those commitments.

The changes are split into two commits: eager writes, then the cap increase. At 64 subscriptions, the pending-output allowance grows from 4 MiB to 32 MiB. ADR-0004 records the sizing decision.

title: Carry Fulu `kzg_commitments` on `data_column_sidecar` events
body:
The application boundary reads commitments from the acquired Fulu sidecar. These will be streamed as an ordered `kzg_commitments` list in `data_column_sidecar` events, following [beacon-APIs v4.0.0](https://github.com/ethereum/beacon-APIs/blob/v4.0.0/apis/eventstream/index.yaml). Each 48-byte commitment is encoded as a 0x-prefixed string of 96 hexadecimal digits. Gloas events omit the field, matching [v5.0.0-alpha.2](https://github.com/ethereum/beacon-APIs/blob/v5.0.0-alpha.2/apis/eventstream/index.yaml).

This supplies the nonempty list required by the [inspected go-eth2-client decoder](https://github.com/attestantio/go-eth2-client/blob/85ac0f6e00e8230c030d9756350ea5e4acd52d2c/api/v1/datacolumnsidecarevent.go). Since Gloas events do not supply `kzg_commitments`, the decoder is incompatible with Gloas. [Lighthouse v8.2.2](https://github.com/sigp/lighthouse/blob/v8.2.2/common/eth2/src/types.rs#L1020-L1028) also requires an additional `versioned_hashes` field, so its decoder remains incompatible.

This change builds on eager SSE writes and the 512 KiB send cap. With no earlier event backlog, that accommodates one block’s 128 column events carrying 21 commitments each, even when the socket accepts no bytes.

title: Report stalled sync status without stopping gossip imports
body:
Control could keep reporting `Following` after block imports stopped and peers disappeared or fell behind. This is an old bug exposed by #261, which removed the Beacon API's independent wall-clock lag check. That check had masked Control's failure to report that the node was no longer synced.

Add `SyncUpdate::Stalled` so Control can report that the node is not synced without stopping slot ticks or gossip imports. The API reports syncing and the distance to the wall slot; coverage recovery or suitable peer claims can restore following. Cached level-peer claims still preserve sync status, allowing a quiet chain but also equally stale peers.

Add `SyncUpdate::is_syncing()`, which returns `true` for `SyncingHead` and `SyncingFinalized`, and `false` for `Following` and `Stalled`. Tiles use it to keep processing gossip and slot ticks while stalled. The Beacon API still reports stalled nodes as syncing because its response describes whether the node is synced.

title: tcache: producer floors and consumer tails
body:
This adds a mechanism for consumers to accurately set their tail value without skipping `TCacheRead`s that arrive out of order:

- every `TCacheRead` now includes an emitter id and a `floor` value
- every producer also periodically publishes their floor value in `TCacheHead` 
- for tiles that read, store and forward `TCacheRead`s, the `floor` is their own consumer tail.

the value of `floor` means: I will not produce an event containing a `TCacheRead` with a `seq` lower than `floor`.

- readers track the received `floor`s per `TCache` per emitting `Tile` (emitters); combined with the locally acquired reads this is used to calculate the tail
- idle consumers read the producer's published floor, so they follow the producer

This mechanism has the following consequences:
- all `TCacheRead`s that are held or stored across tile loops must be acquired
- readers declare expected emitters when constructing consumers (in `Tile::try_init()`)
- producers call `.loop_start()` at the start of every tile loop - this fixes the producer's `floor` for the current loop

title: Slashing pool for block proposals
body:
Offer slashing proofs accepted by gossip to a bounded pool for block proposals.

- **Storage:** `silver_slashing`, owned by the beacon-state tile, holds up to 128 proposer and 16 attester slashings. At capacity, a proof replaces the least valuable of its kind only if it can slash more effective balance on the head.
- **Selection:** choose up to 16 proofs against distinct proposers, then one attester slashing ranked without those proposers. This follows block processing order and excludes attester slashings left with nobody to slash.
- **Signature validity:** refuse attester proofs with signers outside the finalized registry, whose keys may differ across forks. Record each proof's signing fork versions and skip it if the proposal state derives different versions.
- **Pruning:** remove proofs once every offender is slashed or withdrawable in the finalized state. Inclusion on the head alone does not remove a proof, so it remains available after a reorg unless evicted.

Not in this PR: equivocation detection, publishing our own proofs, and the `POST /eth/v{1,2}/beacon/pool/*_slashings` endpoints.

Tile tests cover gossip admission and finalization pruning. A selection test runs signature verification and both slashing passes in block order. It also rejects an overlapping attester proof and a forged signature.

title: Use branch-aware shufflings for attestation verification
body:
Attestation verification caches committees by epoch and RANDAO mix, although their computation also depends on the active validator set, which in turn depends on duty-dependent root. This PR keys shufflings and their aggregate public keys by epoch and duty-dependent root, sharing those entries across verification, block construction, and API publication.

**Before this change, attestation verification could use invalid shufflings, i.e. not matching the active validator set.**

With this change, we enforce that selected shufflings match the identity `(target epoch, duty-dependent root)`. Since we pre-calculate the shufflings both inside  `precompute_for_next_block` and `slot_tick`, that cost is unlikely to be incurred inside the attestation verification critical path.

I've run synthetic benchmarks to validate the cost of cache changes - an individual attestation verification is ~ 0.15% more expensive (i.e. by ~100ns, at the total cost ~70μs) but the batch verification is about the same or cheaper.

title: Batched BLS12-381 point checks with AVX-512 IFMA
body:
This PR adds `bls_simd` crate, implementing `silver_bls_simd::decompress_g2` function identical to both `blst_p2_uncompress` followed by `blst_p2_affine_in_g2` - a single cryptographic operation performing both signature decoding and subgroup check. This is enabled by `simd` feature in the new crate, exposed as enabled by default `bls_simd` in project-level Cargo.toml 

When `simd` feature is enabled and the binary runs on supported CPUs (checked in runtime), silver will batch signature decoding and subgroup checks across eight AVX-512 IFMA lanes, delegating to `decompress_g2::decompress`. 

On a mainnet supernode, non-empty flushes of 8–64 votes took between 24–48% (depending on batch size) less time. Before the change, about 57.5% of all votes went through full 1,024-vote flushes (i.e. the queue was full); with the new simd operation, half of all votes were in flushes of 37 votes or more, and the full 1,024-vote flush affected 0.3% of votes only. The median 32-vote flush took 1.6 ms with simd, versus 2.8 ms before, leaving less time for votes to queue up.

**Note**: occasionally "fused kernel" or in short "kernel" is used both in unit tests code and in comments under `crates/bls_simd` - it stands for "simd implementation core" - do not confuse with operating system internals.

title: Add a Lean proof of `decompress_g2::decompress`
body:
This PR adds a Lean correctness proof for the AVX-512 IFMA core reached through `decompress_g2::decompress` in `crates/bls_simd/src/decompress_g2.rs`. The core decodes and subgroup-checks eight compressed G2 points at once, providing a SIMD alternative to blst.

The proof establishes that the Lean code generated from Rust by Charon and Aeneas returns exactly the result of a hand-written model. On every lane the core decides, that result agrees with the Ethereum cryptography specification’s G2 decoding and subgroup check. Shared test vectors compare the compiled Rust, generated Lean code, and model on recorded inputs; they provide evidence for the translation and hand-written intrinsic definitions.

The proof includes Scott subgroup-check completeness for every point on the concrete BLS12-381 twist. It proves the required point-count bounds and discharges the completeness premise in the extracted correctness theorem.

Two READMEs document the proof:

- `proof/README.md` describes the guarantees, trust boundaries, and verification commands.
- `proof/lean/README.md` explains how to maintain the proof when the SIMD implementation changes.

The proof does not cover the caller in `crates/bls_simd/src/lib.rs` or the blst fallback for undecided lanes. Its connection to compiled Rust relies on extraction, the hand-written external definitions, and the compiler and execution environment.

**Note** the proof, its source files and README files use term "kernel" to mean specific SIMD calculation implemented in this crate. It is *entirely unrelated to operating system internals*.
author: Bronek

title: Make the G2 decompression kernel translatable by Aeneas
body:
Charon and Aeneas can now translate `decompress_g2::decompress` and every function it calls into Lean. Aeneas cannot translate iterator adaptors, so those loops become index loops:

- `iter_mut().enumerate()` and `iter().enumerate()` loops index directly.
- Loops over `(0..n).rev()` count down with while loops.
- `Z_BITS.contains(&bit)` becomes five comparisons.
- `reduce_row` calls `muladd_row`, since IFMA products commute.
- The `blst_p2_affine` for each lane is built in a helper, point. Aeneas silently dropped the last field write when the struct was built inside the loop body.

The new `#[inline]` hints change LLVM's inlining: `scott_membership` is now inlined into `decompress`, and `times_minus_z` stays out of line. Without them, the loop changes alone measured about 0.25% slower. A crate-level allow covers clippy's `needless_range_loop`, with the reason.

`g2_parse` in `crates/beacon_state/tile/benches/bls_verify.rs`, isolated core of a Ryzen 9 9950X, four interleaved runs per binary, mean of means:

    row          main        this change
    simd/8       98.26 us    98.10 us   (-0.16%)
    simd/16      196.56 us   196.06 us  (-0.25%)
    simd/1024    12.579 ms   12.545 ms  (-0.27%)
    blst rows    within -0.15% to +0.12%

Part of the gain is likely code layout, which unrelated changes can move.

title: Prove and use KZG cell operations in silver_crypto_simd
body:
Adds a `kzg` module to `silver_crypto_simd`. It has two public types: `CellBatchVerifier`, which verifies batches of cell proofs, and `CellExtender`, which computes the 128 cells of a blob. Migrates Silver from c-kzg to the new module (except for unit tests and benchmarks).

Also adds a proof in `crates/crypto_simd/proof/` for the whole of `kzg`:

- `CellBatchVerifier::verify` returns `true` exactly when the spec's `verifyCellKzgProofBatch` does.
- `CellExtender::compute` returns `true` exactly when every blob element is canonical. It then writes the spec's `computeCells`, as bytes. On `false`, the cells are unchanged, and the spec returns an error.

Both theorems assume the blst operation contracts in `BlstCorrect`. The extender adds one serialization law, `FrToBytesCorrect`, and the verifier the existing G1 scalar premise. The axiom guard checks 1,621 theorems and nine generated entry points, using only `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`.

Changes in silver:

- `KzgScratch` owns a `CellBatchVerifier`; batch and single re-checks both go through `kzg_verify_batch_multi`.
- `CellScratch` owns a `CellExtender`. The proposal and EL paths take plain byte cells.
- c-kzg is now only a dev-dependency, for tests and the benchmark. The `silver` binary no longer links it.
- The top-level feature `bls_simd` is renamed `crypto_simd`.

`kzg_simd_vs_ckzg` performance bench on the DA capture, Ryzen 9 9950X, best of 5 repetitions:

| Workload | c-kzg | crypto_simd | Speed-up |
|---|---|---|---|
| cells, per blob (78 blobs) | 1,749 µs | 1,376 µs | 1.27× |
| verify, 1 column (18 cells) | 3.90 ms | 3.11 ms | 1.25× |
| verify, 128 columns (2,304 cells) | 117.1 ms | 65.3 ms | 1.80× |

title: AVX-512 IFMA cell extension, verifier and BLS decompression
body:
This PR moves the remaining hot KZG and BLS paths in `silver_crypto_simd` onto AVX-512 IFMA accelerated code. All production code is extracted with Aeneas/Charon and proved against the specification in Lean. Hosts without IFMA keep the existing scalar route.

The PR includes ~41300 lines of Lean proofs of correctness, ~2600 lines of production code in both KZG and BLS, ~2100 lines of unit tests.

- **Cell extension:** an eight-lane Fr FFT (`Fft8`) replaces the scalar transform. It uses lazy reduction through the inverse FFT, transposed short stages, products interleaved with reductions, and vectorised byte conversion.
- **Cell verification:** cells are decoded and interpolated on the same `Fr8`/`Fft8`. All four multi-scalar multiplications run on a new eight-lane Pippenger (`Msm8`), with signed-digit buckets, batched affine additions and GLV. The IFMA route no longer calls blst's multi-scalar multiplication.
- **BLS decompression and subgroup checks:** early-carry Montgomery reduction, dedicated squaring, and lazy `Fp8`/`Fp2x8` arithmetic in reordered G1/G2 formulas.
- **Proofs:** the headline theorems keep their statements. The only axioms are `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`. Each step was proved and then independently reviewed, including mutation controls on the generated code.

### Performance

Measured on Ryzen 9 9950X against `main`.

| | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Cell extension, per blob | 1,377 µs | ~85 µs |
| Verify, 1 column | 3.11 ms | 1.62 ms |
| Verify, 128 columns | 65.3 ms | 27.7 ms |
| G1 decompress + subgroup check, per point | 8.38 µs | 6.43 µs |
| G2 decompress + subgroup check, per point | 11.77 µs | 9.62 µs |
| `g2_parse`, 1024 signatures | 12.22 ms | 10.00 ms |

title: Prove `silver_crypto_simd`'s KZG verifier and move its pairing onto IFMA lanes
body:
This PR changes `silver_crypto_simd` to verify and extend PeerDAS cells with AVX-512 IFMA lane kernels where the CPU has them. On other CPUs, each operation takes whichever implementation is faster: portable Rust or blst.

## What changes in `src/`

Each operation picks its route at run time, based on available CPU features:

| Check | CPU features | Selects | Otherwise |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ifma_available()` (was `simd_available`) | `simd` feature + AVX-512F + AVX-512 IFMA | IFMA lane kernels: G1/G2 decoding, the verifier's MSMs, sums and pairing, cell extension | portable MSM and field arithmetic; blst G1 decoding and KZG pairing |
| `sha_available()` | SHA + SSE4.1 | SHA-NI for the KZG challenge hash, on either route | SHA-256 in plain Rust |
| `bmi2_available()` | BMI2 | the `mulx` build of the portable `Fp` product | the same Rust for baseline x86-64 |

The checks are independent. CPUs without AVX-512 IFMA but with SHA-NI, for example AMD Zen 1–3, take the portable route with the SHA-NI hash.

- **`bls/`, the IFMA route:**
  - the verifier's sums and pairing run on `Fp8` lanes;
  - a two-pair Miller loop on precomputed lines, generated by `gen_pairing_lines.py` into `kzg/pairing_lines.rs`, needs no inversion;
  - the final exponentiation runs on lanes too. It computes the spec's value cubed, as blst's does; gcd(3, r) = 1, so the verdict is the spec's.
- **`portable/`, new:** a scalar `Fp` in blst's six-word layout, G1 arithmetic, a G1 decoder and the verifier's MSMs. Without IFMA, the MSMs run here. On IFMA CPUs, the decoder handles undecided lanes and batches shorter than eight.
- **blst without IFMA:** G1 decoding and the KZG pairing check call blst, because blst is faster for both. The pairing wrapper drops pairs with a point at infinity, as the spec's `pairingCheck` does.
- **`sha256/`, new:** SHA-256 with a SHA-NI path. The challenge absorbs its preimage in parts.
- **`kzg/`:** the setup's G2 points, Fr constants and coset inverses are literals, and scalar `Fr` arithmetic replaces blst's.

## Performance

Medians on one isolated Zen 5 core (Ryzen 9 9950X), comparing `main` → this branch:

| Operation | without IFMA | with IFMA |
|---|---|---|
| verify, 1 column | 3.93 → 3.37 ms (−14%) | 1.66 → 1.37 ms (−17%) |
| verify, 8 columns | 11.31 → 9.84 ms (−13%) | 3.31 → 3.03 ms (−9%) |
| verify, 128 columns | 120.5 → 107.8 ms (−11%) | 27.78 → 27.25 ms (−2%) |
| cells per blob | 1.42 → 1.23 ms (−14%) | 85.8 µs, unchanged |
| verifier construction | 2.37 → 2.19 ms (−7%) | 1.10 → 0.85 ms (−23%) |

Without IFMA, this compares software on the same hardware; SHA-NI with SSE4.1, and BMI2, are still used. With IFMA, moving the pairing onto lanes saves about 0.29 ms per batch, so the gain is largest for small batches.

## Changes visible to callers

- `simd_available` is renamed `ifma_available`.
- `bls::uncompress_in_g1_blst` is public; it is the G1 decoder used without IFMA.
- `bls::{fp12, pairing, glv, miller_lines}` and `msm8` are crate-private.
- The limb helpers moved to `bls::limbs`.
- The IFMA kernel modules stay `pub` for the `kzg_simd_phases` benchmark, but are `#[doc(hidden)]`.
- aarch64 takes the non-IFMA route. It is checked by clippy and a test build, but neither measured nor proved.
- `crates/crypto_simd/README.md` is new. It covers the crate's purpose, main APIs, CPU features, uses of blst and how to reuse the crate.

## Proofs (`proof/`)

- **How:** Charon and Aeneas translate the x86-64 build to Lean, with the intrinsics as models. The generated code is proved equal to EthLib's spec. The spec is pinned to a fork commit for ethereum/EthLib#52, tagged `silver-pin-5d7ab0f`.
- **Kept in sync:** CI's `extract.sh --check` fails if the Rust and the extraction differ.
- **With IFMA:** `verify_eq_spec_ifma` and `verify_eq_upstream_ifma` have no blst premise. The extender headlines have none on either route.
- **Without IFMA:** the general headlines take two scoped laws about blst:
  - G1 decoding agrees with the spec, required only when IFMA is unavailable;
  - the two-pair pairing check agrees with the spec on the two fixed KZG G2 points, required only for a state that stores the scalar workspace.
- **Laws are consistent:** a control builds an instance satisfying both laws from the spec. It shows consistency, not that blst satisfies them.
- **Proved components:** lane pairing, scalar `Fr`, SHA-256, both MSMs, the portable G1 decoder and the Scott subgroup criteria. The axioms are only Lean's three standard ones; there is no `sorry` and no `native_decide`.
- **Not proved:** blst's G1 decoder and pairing (the laws above), the G2 decoder's blst fallback used by signatures, and aarch64.
- **Details:** `proof/README.md`.
- **Licence:** `proof/lean/` is CC0, so others can reuse the proofs without attribution. The rest stays MIT.

## Notes

- **CI memory:** the cold proof build peaks at 14.62 GiB in one Lean process, against the runner's 16 GB.
- **Workflow:** the proof workflow now requires SHA-NI and SSE4.1, besides IFMA, before it demands kernel replay.

title: Validate BLS public keys before verifying signatures
body:
Fixes CL-168.

The spec's `bls.Verify` requires `KeyValidate` for every public key, which rejects point at infinity or outside G1. Before this change, we only decoded keys with `PublicKey::from_bytes`, without the required validation. Affected paths:

- validator keys loaded from state bytes without a pubkey sidecar (`FinalizedValidators::try_new`);
- the builder key of an execution payload bid (`bid_signing_input`);
- the `from_bls_pubkey` of a BLS-to-execution change.

Keys loaded from a sidecar are not re-validated. Silver writes the sidecar from keys it has already validated, so it is trusted.

## Cost

Timings over the 2,314,978 validator keys of the mainnet perf fixture:

| Boot | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| without a sidecar (checkpoint sync, first boot) | 17.1 s | 71.2 s |
| with a sidecar | 0.44 s | 0.44 s |

In this PR we are paying an extra ~54s when booting the node from checkpoint (i.e. sidecar not present). Re-validating the sidecar on every restart would cost the same, and we do **not** do it - instead we treat it as trusted.  A follow-up PR will bring key decoding on IFMA hosts down to ~ 15 s (from ~ 71 s), by switching to accelerated decompression and validation.

Each bid and BLS-to-execution change adds about 23 µs, at most about 0.4 ms per block.

## Upgrade note

A sidecar written by an older binary may hold unvalidated keys. Delete the `<slot>.pubkeys` files in the checkpoint directory once after upgrading. The next boot decodes the keys from the state, validates them, and later checkpoints write a validated sidecar.

title: Typed BLS G1 and G2 points, IFMA acceleration for batched signature checks
body:
This is the final PR of planned `crypto_simd` IFMA acceleration features. It moves pairing checks in `SigBatch` and `verify_one_checked` to `silver_crypto_simd` on IFMA CPUs (without IFMA, signature pairing stays on blst).

Added to `crypto_simd`:

* `G1Point` and `G2Point` represent canonical, on-curve points in the prime-order subgroup, including infinity.
* `PairingProduct` processes lane sets of eight pairs, followed by one final exponentiation. Any active lane with zero output Z makes the whole product fall back to blst.

`crates/crypto_simd/README.md` documents the point and pairing-product API.

Changed in `beacon_state`: `CheckedSignature` now wraps a `G2Point`.

## Keys

As on `main`, cached keys and per-message key sums get no per-verification subgroup check. They now enter `PairingProduct` through `G1Point::from_trusted`, which makes that trust explicit. This relies on key admission:

- record keys validated at load, by #431 and #433;
- deposit keys validated by `PublicKey::key_validate` in `is_valid_deposit_signature`;
- sidecar keys written from the cache and trusted on load.

## Proofs

Lean 4.29.1 checks the Charon/Aeneas extraction against EthLib's executable spec (`gattaca-com/EthLib` `5d7ab0f`, tag `silver-pin-5d7ab0f`; need resolution of https://github.com/ethereum/EthLib/issues/52 before switch to `ethereum/EthLib`)

- Decoder list theorems also establish `Kzg.G1AffineValid` / `Kzg.G2AffineValid` for accepted points. Decoder and KZG headlines gain no premises. G1 keeps #427's scoped non-IFMA law.
- `build_is_one_correct` and `two_pairs_are_one_correct` prove agreement with `pairingCheck` under their stated premises, including for infinity pairs. They use `RuntimeFeatures`, explicit point validity and `PairingProduct.BlstMatchesSpec` for the blst arm. `controls/downstream/PairingSmoke.lean` satisfies all premises at once.

Trusted, not proved:

- `PairingProduct.BlstMatchesSpec`: the whole blst wrapper agrees with `pairingCheck` on finite, canonical subgroup pairs. Raw `blst_miller_loop_n` does not skip G2 infinity. This law is separate from #427's KZG pairing law.
- `ConstructorsMatchSpec` for `from_blst`, and `OperationsMatchSpec` for hash to G2, weighted sums and the negated generator.

Dependency checks exclude these three laws from KZG and decoder headlines. Random-weight batching, key admission and hash-to-G2 correctness remain unproved.

## Benchmarks

`SigBatch::verify_all` from `bls_verify`, comparing `main` (`621899ff`) with this branch. Medians of five rotated rounds on isolated core 14 (AMD Ryzen 9 9950X), with IFMA:

| Workload | `main` µs | branch µs | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1-vote flush | 448.8 | 237.3 | −47% |
| 2-vote flush | 651.8 | 361.9 | −44% |
| 16-vote flush | 997.2 | 703.4 | −29% |
| 256 votes, 2 signing roots | 3,550.8 | 3,257.4 | −8% |
| 256 votes, 256 signing roots | 34,053 | 15,979 | −53% |
| Synthetic block-shaped batch, 106 entries | 14,459 | 6,879 | −52% |

The flush cases use at most two signing roots.

On a mainnet supernode (EPYC 4585PX), mean `verify_all` time per single-vote flush was 48% lower. Total `verify_all` time per slot was 12% lower. Single-vote flushes increased from 39% to 49% of flushes (shorter flush times cause more frequent *and* smaller flushes).

title: Declare hashtree_init as returning nothing
body:
hashtree's C `hashtree_init` returns `void` (`hashtree.h`: `void hashtree_init(hashtree_hash_fcn override)`). Our binding declared it as returning `c_int` and debug-asserted that the result was 1. Calling a `void` function through a signature that returns `c_int` reads whatever value is left in the return register. That value depends on the code path hashtree's CPU detection took, so it varies from machine to machine.

As a result, debug builds sometimes panic with `hashtree_init() failed` on first use of the hasher, and after that the `LazyLock` is poisoned. Hashing itself is unaffected: detection always falls back to a working backend. Silver's own `just test` uses the `release-with-debug` profile, where debug assertions are off, so it never hit this. Downstream crates that run `cargo test` in debug do. The helix relay's unit tests fail this way on some GitHub runners (reading 2) and on Apple silicon (reading 0), while hashing produces the correct digest.

The binding now declares `hashtree_init` with no return value, matching the C prototype, and the assertion is removed because there is no status to check.

title: Bound per-connection QUIC and req/resp resources
body:
Stacked on #446, since both change the snappy decoder. Retarget to `main` once #446 merges.

## Summary

Bounds the resources a single connection can hold in the QUIC transport and the req/resp codecs.

- **QUIC transport config**
  - Cap the connection receive window at 16 MiB. quinn's default is unbounded; rust-libp2p uses 15 MB.
  - The window must stay above the bandwidth-delay product. 16 MiB allows about 80 MB/s per peer at 200 ms RTT.
  - Allow zero unidirectional streams and no datagram buffer. libp2p uses neither.
- **Inbound gossip stream**
  - When a new inbound gossip stream is negotiated, close the previous one, as rust-libp2p and go-libp2p-pubsub do.
  - This releases its tcache reservation.
- **`DataColumnSidecarsByRoot` requests**
  - Bound them at the spec maximum, 136,192 bytes, instead of `MAX_PAYLOAD_SIZE`.
  - This matches Lighthouse.
- **RPC error responses**
  - Reject a declared length above the 256-byte `ErrorMessage` limit before reading the body.
- **Snappy framing**
  - Bound the framed bytes per chunk at `max_compressed_len(n)` plus framing overhead.
  - Lighthouse applies a stricter bound to the whole stream, so interoperating encoders fit.
  - The cost is one add and one compare per frame header.

## Testing

- Each change has a test.
- `silver_network` and `silver_ssz` tests pass.

title: Validate addresses before admitting inbound QUIC connections under load
body:
## Summary

Inbound admission moves into `p2p/admission.rs` (`InboundAdmission`). Under load, it uses QUIC's stateless Retry to validate a source address before creating any connection state.

- **Trusted-IP bypass**
  - Over the cap, a trusted source passes a Retry first.
  - Trusted overflow is bounded at twice the cap, the size of the peer manager's slot table.
- **Handshakes in flight**
  - These are now counted until they complete or close.
  - An unvalidated Initial gets a Retry when 16 or more handshakes are in flight, or when fewer than 16 slots remain.
- **Per-IP limit**
  - At most 8 inbound connections per IPv4 address or IPv6 /64. This leaves room for several nodes behind one NAT.
  - Trusted IPs and loopback are exempt.
  - An unvalidated repeat source gets a Retry first.
- **Logging**
  - `Endpoint::accept` failures log at `debug!` instead of `error!`.
- **New counter**
  - `NetworkCounters::InboundRetried`.

A Retry costs a peer one extra round trip, and only in the states above.

## Testing

- In-process endpoint tests cover the trusted bypass and handshake-in-flight paths.
- Unit tests cover `InboundAdmission`.
- `silver_network` tests pass.

title: discv5: match responses to requests, tighten IP voting and table admission
body:
## Summary

Aligns several discv5 paths more closely with the wire spec and sigp/discv5. There is one commit per change.

- **WHOAREYOU:**
  - Accept one only if it echoes the nonce of a recent request we sent, from that request's address, per the wire spec.
  - Request nonces are kept for 2 seconds, longer than `request_timeout`, so peers with slower round trips still complete handshakes.
  - A mismatch no longer consumes the pending probe.
- **NODES:**
  - Accept only replies to our own outstanding FINDNODE.
  - Each node must sit at a requested distance.
  - At most 16 packets per request.
  - A record never replaces one with a higher `seq`.
- **IP voting:**
  - Votes expire after 30 minutes, as in sigp/discv5.
  - An address needs the threshold plus a strict majority of live votes.
  - Votes are dropped on eviction or ban.
  - The default threshold is unchanged.
- **Routing table:**
  - A handshake peer enters the table only if its ENR advertises the packet source, as in sigp/discv5.
  - Insertion uses the normal path, so a full bucket parks it as pending.
  - The session is kept either way, and session peers outside the table now get answers. Nodes behind NAT keep working.
- **Sessions:** record a nonce and refresh `last_active` only after decryption succeeds.
- **Challenges:** key them by node id and address. The per-IP WHOAREYOU limit groups IPv6 by /64.
- **Decoding:**
  - Handshake ENRs must decode exactly.
  - PONG ports are decoded as `u16`.
  - Handshake signature and key sizes must be 64 and 33.
- **Bookkeeping:** the fork-digest tally is capped at 64 entries.

## Testing

- Each change has unit tests.
- `silver_discovery` unit and e2e tests pass.

  - Maps and sets keyed by `MessageId` now use a per-process seeded `foldhash`. Before, they used the id's first 8 bytes.
  - The pre-decompression fast-dedup hash is keyed the same way. A hit there counts as a duplicate without comparing content.
  - `MessageId` hashes as two fixed-width writes.
- **IWANT serving**
  - At most `max_ihave_length` IWANT ids per peer per heartbeat, the most a compliant peer requests.
  - The per-id retransmission filter is shared with IDONTWANT. So IDONTWANT recording is capped at 1000 ids per peer per heartbeat.
- **Topic parsing:** subnet ids must be canonical decimal, so each topic has one spelling and one message id.
- **Invalid snappy bodies:** these are now deduped and penalised like bodies with a bad length.

## Performance

Measured with ad-hoc benchmarks:

| Case | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `DedupCache::has` miss, per id | 45–47 ns | 45–52 ns |
| Map insert, per id | 4.2–6.1 ns | 5.6–8.6 ns |
| Fast hash, 2 KiB payload | 458 ns | 83 ns |
| Fast hash, 128 KiB payload | 30.3 µs | 4.3–6.2 µs |

## Testing

- Each change has a test.
- `silver_common`, `silver_gossip`, `silver_peer` and `silver_control` tests pass.

title: Bound request parsing, buffering and receive time in the API server
body:
## Summary

- **Head parsing**
  - `dispatch` parsed the whole buffered head on every read until it completed.
  - It now parses only once the buffered bytes can contain the end of the head, searching each byte once. It also parses each time the buffer doubles, so malformed heads are still rejected early, at linear total cost.
  - Heads are capped at 4 MiB, answered with 431. That still fits the 32K-id validator queries a GET may carry; a const assert keeps the two limits in step.
- **Read buffer size**
  - `read_buf` kept its peak size, up to 16 MiB, for the life of a connection.
  - Once a request is consumed and the buffer is empty, it returns to 4 KiB if it grew past 64 KiB.
- **Request deadline**
  - Requests had only the 75 s idle timeout, refreshed by any byte.
  - A request must now arrive in full within 60 s of its first byte, or it gets 408 and the connection lingers as for other rejects. A 16 MiB body needs about 2.2 Mbit/s.
  - The wait between keep-alive requests is unchanged.

## Testing

- New tests cover linear-time head parsing, the 431 limit, buffer release and the 408 deadline. Each fails without its fix.
- Guard tests cover long queries, leading empty lines, early rejection of non-HTTP bytes, buffer reuse and keep-alive waits.
- `silver_httpcore` and `silver_beacon_api` tests pass.

title: Bound API submissions and proposer preparations
body:
Stacked on #452, since both change the connection loop in `beacon_api/src/server.rs`. Retarget to `main` once that PR merges.

## Summary

- **Submission size**
  - Each entry of a submission becomes one message on the `beacon_api_requests` queue (capacity 2^14), and lists could hold up to 256K entries.
  - A submission may now carry at most 4096 entries; larger bodies get 400. That is a quarter of the queue, and one slot's attestations for 131,072 validators.
  - This applies to every multi-entry submission: attestations, sync committee messages, aggregates, contributions, payload attestations, BLS changes and proposer preferences. Larger BLS-change batches need splitting.
- **Outstanding messages**
  - At most 8192 messages (half the queue) may await verdicts across all connections; a request that would exceed this gets 503.
  - A single-entry submission, such as a block, is always admitted.
  - The total is derived from each connection's pending state, so it is released as verdicts arrive or connections close and cannot drift.
- **Proposer preparations**
  - `prepare_beacon_proposer` entries whose index is at or beyond the head registry length are dropped, and the request still gets 200, as Lighthouse does.
  - Validators pending activation already have registry indices.

## Testing

- New tests cover the per-request cap, the 503 budget (including release on verdicts and on reaping, and the single-entry exemption) and dropped preparations. Each fails without its fix.
- `silver_beacon_api` tests pass.

title: Validate builder URLs and refuse line breaks in client request heads
body:
## Summary

- **Builder URLs**
  - These were checked only for UTF-8 or an `http://` prefix, and their path was copied into the request line as written.
  - A new `plain_http_url` in `silver_pbs` accepts only printable ASCII, an `http://` or `https://` scheme, and a non-empty host.
  - It is applied to builder preference entries, builder configs used for bid requests, and the `Eth-Builder-Url` header on block submission.
  - Preference entries that fail are reported per entry, so the API answers 400 with indexed failures. Bid requests skip such entries, and block submission does not forward to them.
- **`frame_request`**
  - It now returns an error, without writing anything, if the path, `Host` or any header name or value contains CR or LF.
  - `HttpPool` keeps such a request on its connection and fails it on the next dispatch. Callers that gate on capacity therefore don't send it again.

## Testing

- New tests cover URL acceptance, preference entries without a plain URL, `Eth-Builder-Url` forwarding, `frame_request` refusal and pool reuse after a refused request. Each fails without its fix.
- `silver_pbs`, `silver_httpcore` and `silver_beacon_api` tests pass.

title: Use JSON bid version when the HTTP header is absent
body:
## Summary

Silver's JSON bid adapter converts the bid to SSZ but discards the envelope's `version`. Without an `Eth-Consensus-Version` header, the fork check then rejects an otherwise valid Fulu bid.

Keep the JSON version and use it only when the HTTP header is absent. A present header still takes precedence, and SSZ responses still require their own header. Existing bid validation and Gloas handling are unchanged.

Adds tests with signed JSON and SSZ bids, local HTTP callbacks, header precedence, and decoder reuse.
